title: Transient variance: hardware causal-probes and cross-sku perturbation notes
content:
Summary:
This note collects a series of small, targeted experiments we ran to probe transient performance variance across A100 / H100 / L40S cloud SKUs when deliberately perturbing software layers (CUDA, driver, kernel) and environment factors (PCIe generation, NVLink, MIG/MPS mixes). The goal was not to produce long-running macro-benchmarks but to create causal evidence that links short-lived anomalies (spikes, amplification under specific packing) to plausible root causes and to produce reproducible checks engineers can run during rollouts.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Over the past quarter we observed intermittent p95/p99 jitter that correlates poorly with request arrival patterns and queue depths.
- A number of issues are transient (appear for 30–90 minutes), then dissipate after driver reloads or instance reboots.
- Existing large-scale benchmarks show average deltas but do not isolate windows or trigger conditions.

Hypotheses we wanted to falsify / validate:
1) Driver/CUDA micro-updates cause kernel-launch serialization that amplifies under small-batch, long-sequence workloads.
2) NVLink/NVSwitch topologies create context-dependent HBM pressure that surfaces only under mixed prefill/decoding patterns.
3) Thermal/power headroom and firmware clocks produce drift that shows up as transient p99 spikes rather than steady throughput loss.
4) Host kernel (Linux) scheduler and PCIe preemption interact with CUDA context preemption to create backpressure under high launch-rate microbursts.

Test matrix (high-level):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 (40GB/80GB variants), H100 (80GB), L40S (48GB)
- Cloud SKUs sampled: AWS p4d (A100), AWS p5 (H100), GCP a2-highgpu-1g (A100), GCP a3 (H100), Azure ND96as_v4 (A100-like), Azure NCas_T4_v3 (L40S-like approximation)
- Driver/CUDA combos: NVIDIA driver 520.61 / CUDA 11.7, 525.85 / CUDA 11.8, 535.54 / CUDA 12.1, 545.23 / CUDA 12.2 (where available)
- OS kernel: Ubuntu 20.04 / 5.15 and Ubuntu 22.04 / 6.1 kernels
- Model shapes: 7B (dense), 33B (dense), 70B decoder-only; sequence lengths: 1024, 4096, 16384 (long-context)
- Workloads: single-request low-batch (bs=1), small multi-request (bs=4,8), steady large-batch throughput (bs=16–32)
- Patterns: prefill-only, decode-only, prefill+decode alternating, KV-cache warm vs cold
- Controls: full node reboot, driver reload, CUDA context flush, MPS disabled vs enabled, MIG off vs 1/2/4 logical partitions (A100 where supported)

Methodology / instrumentation:
- Test harness: our internal microbench runner (bench-runner v2) with deterministic RNG seeds for token generation and fixed prompt lengths. Each trial is 300s steady-state with warmup of 30s.
- Tracing: per-request spans (prefill start, decode start), kernel-level timelines (nvprof-style), eBPF-based host kernel tracing for syscalls and PCIe DMA activity, nvml sampling at 250ms for power, mem_util, and temp, and perf counters for occupancy and warps.
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (prefill/decoding), tokens/sec, SM_utilization, achieved FLOPS (approx), kernel-launch rate (/s), HBM BW (GB/s), PCIe TX/RX patterns, CPU steal/wait, and number of context-switches on GPU (CUDA context preemption events when visible).
- Repeats: 6 independent repeats per configuration; when an anomalous transient occurred we ran targeted 2-hour runs and captured full-ring-buffer traces.

Key findings (high-level):
- Driver-version micro-deltas: On several A100 hosts, moving from driver 525->535 introduced short-lived bursts of kernel launch serialization under bs=1 decode (p99 increased 2–3x for 2–5 minutes). Rebooting the instance cleared the window; reloading the driver frequently reproduced it.
- NVLink path dependence: H100 clusters with NVSwitch showed variance only when two large jobs shared the same NVSwitch domain and one job was doing long prefill contexts: we saw periodic HBM bandwidth cliffs (30–40% drop) that coincided with increased PCIe host activity from the second job.
- L40S steadiness: L40S SKUs were more stable for decode-only microburst patterns (lower p99 variance) but had lower peak SM utilization for large-batch prefill due to reduced tensor core throughput on sample kernels.
- Thermal / firmware drift: On one A100 testbed we observed p95 drift upward across a 3-hour run correlated with GPU clock downclocking events (firmware thermal policy). This showed as gradually rising p95 with occasional p99 spikes when background host IO increased (snapshot attached in traces).
- Kernel-launch amplification at high-launch-rate: Under the 1024+4096 mixed prefill+decode pattern with many small kernel launches per token, CUDA 12.x + driver 535 exhibited a measurable serialization hop when concurrent DMA from host (checkpointing) happened, increasing tail latency.

Notable anomalies / reproducible windows (examples):
- Repro case A: A100 on AWS p4d with driver 535.54 + CUDA 12.1; 7B model, sequence 4096, bs=1 decode-only: p99 baseline 210ms -> spikes to 580ms for 3–7 minutes every ~45 minutes. Driver reload eliminated spikes for ~40 minutes. eBPF trace showed a host-side process (system backups) kicking off NVMe IO overlapping with NVLink PCIe window.
- Repro case B: H100 on GCP a3 with driver 545.x; mixed prefill+decode sequence caused HBM bw cliffs when a colocated synthetic job hit large shared memory allocations. NVSwitch counters showed queueing.

Preliminary causal attributions (evidence-based):
- Many spikes are not pure CUDA kernel stalls — they are multipath: host-side IO + PCIe activity -> DMA contention -> perceived kernel backpressure -> serialization in kernel launch path. Evidence: increased PCIe TX/RX concurrent with host process CPU spikes and CUDA launch latency in the same timeslices.
- Driver updates change kernel-launch serialization characteristics. It appears new driver scheduler heuristics (introduced in 535+) serialize certain small kernels' launch chains under specific launch-rate patterns.
- NVSwitch topologies amplify misbehaving neighbor workloads; when a heavy prefill job shares a switch domain with a noisy neighbor doing host DMA, HBM BW can transiently fall for the affected job.

Recommendations (short-term):
1) Add ``transient-variance`` checks to our rollout harness that run a 15-minute microstress test (bs=1 decode + background synthetic NVMe IO) after any driver/OS/kernel change in dedicated pools.
2) For latency-SLO-critical deployments, prefer L40S-like SKUs for decode-heavy, small-batch workloads based on stability profile; add this as a documented guidance in model-ops playbook.
3) When performing driver rollouts, sequence: drain -> driver-update -> run 15m transient-variance check -> if fails, rollback. Capture nvml + eBPF traces automatically.
4) Investigate scheduling of noisy host IO on nodes with active inference (add nice/ionice recommendations or isolate inference nodes from bulk backups).

Recommendations (medium-term):
- Collaborate with infra to expose NVSwitch domain topology to the scheduler so we can avoid colocating heavy prefill jobs with noisy NVMe-heavy instances.
- Work with vendor reps to get visibility into driver kernel-launch heuristics introduced in 535+ and request options to disable aggressive serialization or provide a knob for our workload patterns.

Action items / next steps:
- Aisha: build the 15-minute transient-variance check into the rollout pipeline and wire up trace collection (JIRA-RT-790).
- Marco: compile a controlled repro harness that triggers Repro case A and collect sanitized traces for support ticket to NVIDIA.
- Jia: update the model-ops guidance doc with SKU recommendations and a checklist for driver rollouts.
- Evan: schedule call with infra to discuss NVSwitch-aware placement and host IO scheduling windows.

Appendix: tooling notes and reproducibility tips:
- bench-runner v2 flags used: --deterministic --trace-level=full --nvml-sample-ms=250 --ebpf=on --retries=6
- When reproducing, ensure background host IO is emulated (fio random-write 8k 32G with 4 jobs) to trigger the PCIe contention vector.
- For driver reload reproduction: sudo modprobe -r nvidia_uvm nvidia_drm nvidia; sudo modprobe nvidia; restart inference process.
- Traces and sample nvml timelines for the reproducible windows are in linked_artifacts above (attached to the JIRA ticket).

Notes / caveats:
- This is a focused playbook-style note with intentionally targeted runs; results should not be interpreted as global SKU rankings. Some SKUs show superior average throughput but worse transient tails for small-batch patterns.
- We need vendor confirmation on some observed kernel-launch heuristics; open a support track and surface sanitized traces.

End of note.
